slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code accesses and reads local files and YouTube URLs, including hardcoded URL patterns for YouTube and generic HTTP(S) URLs. It uses sensitive file operations (fs.existsSync, fs.createReadStream, node-id3.read) and network operations (node-fetch, ytdl-core) to fetch audio streams and metadata. The code then processes and transcodes audio streams, sends images and text messages, and streams audio data over a WebSocket connection to the hardcoded server wss://zello.io/ws, enabling media streaming and metadata transmission to this external server.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code is a media streaming client that fetches audio and metadata from YouTube URLs, generic HTTP URLs, or local files, processes and transcodes audio streams, and streams them to a known external WebSocket server (wss://zello.io/ws). It uses legitimate libraries (ytdl-core, node-fetch, node-id3, sharp) and performs expected operations for a media streaming application. There is no evidence of obfuscation, code injection, environment manipulation, or unauthorized data exfiltration. The code does not collect sensitive system or user credentials, nor does it upload arbitrary user files to unknown endpoints. The external server is hardcoded but corresponds to a known service (Zello) for voice streaming, not a suspicious or attacker-controlled domain. Compared to the known malicious patterns, this code lacks key indicators such as eval-based payload execution, credential harvesting, or stealthy data exfiltration. The use of network and file APIs is consistent with the intended functionality and not indicative of malware.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, when rsh.js is executed as a detached process, the code collects detailed system, environment, and user information, compresses and encodes it, decompresses an obfuscated payload from a base64 string, sets the NODE_NO_EVAL environment variable to undefined, and executes the decompressed payload using eval, resulting in the execution of further malicious code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting extensive system, environment, and user data, compressing and encoding it, and executing obfuscated code via eval are all strong indicators of malicious intent and are commonly used to evade detection and enable data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not collect and exfiltrate system or user information, nor do they execute dynamically decompressed and obfuscated code via eval.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Compression and system info gathering may be used in legitimate diagnostics or telemetry, but not in combination with obfuscated payload execution and without user consent.
key_indicators: Obfuscated and base64-encoded payload decompressed and executed via eval
Systematic collection of system, environment, and user data
Manipulation of environment variables to bypass security controls
No user notification or consent for data collection or code execution

package_info.why_malicious: All packages in this campaign execute obfuscated JavaScript code at install time, which collects extensive system, environment, and user information and establishes a persistent reverse shell to a remote attacker-controlled server (rsh.51pwn.com:8880), enabling full remote code execution and exfiltration of sensitive data. The attack chain is triggered via multiple npm lifecycle hooks, uses detached background processes for persistence, and employs obfuscation and dynamic code execution to evade detection.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed, triggering preinstall, postinstall, test, or init scripts defined in package.json.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of scripts/init.js

attack_chain.action: scripts/init.js is executed, which launches scripts/rsh.js as a detached child process and immediately exits to conceal ongoing activity.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of scripts/rsh.js in the background

attack_chain.action: scripts/rsh.js collects detailed system, environment, and user data, compresses and encodes it, decompresses an obfuscated payload, and executes it via eval.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of reverse shell payload from decompressed code

attack_chain.action: The reverse shell payload establishes a persistent connection to rsh.51pwn.com:8880, exfiltrates collected system information, and provides the attacker with remote shell access for arbitrary command execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent remote access and control over the compromised system

behavioral_signatures: Execution of scripts/init.js during npm install, test, or init lifecycle events
Creation of detached child processes in install/test scripts (child_process.fork with {detached: true})
Presence of obfuscated or base64-encoded JavaScript payloads in package files
Use of eval to execute dynamically decompressed or generated code
Outbound TCP connections to hardcoded C2 domains (e.g., rsh.51pwn.com:8880) during or after installation
Collection and exfiltration of system, environment, and user data during package installation or execution
file_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript with base64-encoded or Unicode-escaped payloads
network_indicators: Outbound TCP connections to rsh.51pwn.com on port 8880
Initial data exfiltration containing compressed system information
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm packages for execution of scripts during install, test, or init lifecycle events, especially those launching detached child processes or containing obfuscated/base64-encoded code. Flag any package that establishes outbound TCP connections to suspicious domains (e.g., rsh.51pwn.com) or uncommon ports during or after installation. Use static analysis to detect eval usage on dynamically decompressed payloads and the presence of Unicode-escaped or base64-encoded code. Alert on collection and exfiltration of system, environment, or user data during package installation or execution. Correlate file indicators (scripts/init.js, scripts/rsh.js, suspicious package.json scripts) with behavioral and network indicators for high-confidence detection.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code reads sensitive files such as browser login data and environment variables like DISCORD_TOKEN, then exfiltrates this data via HTTPS POST to a remote webhook endpoint controlled by the attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code accesses credential stores and environment variables containing sensitive information, then transmits this data to an external server, which is a hallmark of infostealer malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not access or transmit user credentials or sensitive files without explicit user consent and clear justification.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Security auditing tools may access such files, but only with user awareness, explicit permission, and for legitimate security purposes.
key_indicators: Access to credential stores (browser login data, environment tokens)
Exfiltration of data to webhook.site or similar endpoints
Use of environment variables for sensitive data extraction
Network transmission of credential data without user consent

package_info.package_versions: all published versions of the malicious typosquatted packages
package_info.why_malicious: The packages are part of a coordinated supply chain attack campaign leveraging typosquatting to impersonate legitimate libraries. Upon installation or import, they download and execute infostealer malware (such as Blank Grabber and Skuld Stealer) designed to exfiltrate sensitive data, including credentials and tokens, from infected systems. The packages attempt to appear trustworthy by referencing legitimate tools and use external platforms (GitHub, repl.it) to host and deliver malicious payloads, primarily targeting Windows users.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious typosquatted package, triggering the download and execution of a remote payload.
attack_chain.leads_to: Initial payload download and execution on the victim's system

attack_chain.action: The malicious payload (infostealer) is executed, establishing persistence and preparing to steal sensitive data.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential and data theft capabilities are enabled

attack_chain.action: The infostealer accesses sensitive files and environment variables, exfiltrating the stolen data to attacker-controlled endpoints.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen credentials and sensitive information from the victim's system

behavioral_signatures: Package downloads and executes remote code at import-time or during installation
Access to credential stores (browser login data, environment tokens) by package or payload code
Exfiltration of sensitive data to external endpoints such as webhook.site, GitHub, or repl.it
file_indicators: setup.py or __init__.py containing remote code download and execution logic
Unexpected executable files (e.g., payload.exe, malware.py) created during package installation or import
References to external code hosting platforms (GitHub, repl.it) in package source code
network_indicators: Outbound HTTP/HTTPS requests to raw.githubusercontent.com for payload downloads
Connections to webhook.site or similar data collection endpoints for exfiltration
Downloads from repl.it or other code hosting services during installation or import
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for packages that initiate network connections to code hosting or data exfiltration endpoints during installation or import. Flag any package that downloads and executes remote code, accesses credential stores, or references known infostealer infrastructure. Use static analysis to detect suspicious import-time or setup.py logic, and dynamic analysis to observe unexpected network or filesystem activity during package installation or import. Correlate creation of unexpected executables and outbound connections to known malicious infrastructure.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code uploads arbitrary file data to https://telegra.ph/upload via HTTP POST, sending the file as form-data and returning the resulting URL, enabling silent exfiltration of user files.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated file uploads to external services without user interaction are a hallmark of data exfiltration and are not justified in the context of WhatsApp automation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A WhatsApp automation package should not upload arbitrary files to third-party file-sharing services, especially without user notification or consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: A legitimate file-sharing client or backup tool may upload files, but only with user consent and clear intent.
key_indicators: No user notification or consent before upload
Automated network exfiltration of file data

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains obfuscated JavaScript code that, at runtime, exfiltrates user files to multiple hardcoded external file-sharing services without user consent. It automates unauthorized data uploads to suspicious endpoints, using randomized filenames and evasion techniques, making it a tool for covert data exfiltration and a clear indicator of compromise.

attack_chain.action: Prepare file data for upload by creating form-data with randomized filenames.
attack_chain.leads_to: File data is ready for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Upload file data to external file-sharing services via HTTP POST requests, targeting multiple hardcoded endpoints.

attack_chain.action: Monitor the package file for changes and reload dynamically to evade detection or enable code updates.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code persists and can be updated without user awareness.

behavioral_signatures: Automated creation of form-data from arbitrary file buffers at runtime
Silent HTTP POST requests to known file-sharing endpoints without user interaction
Use of fake or randomized User-Agent headers in network requests to evade detection
Self-watching and hot-reloading of package files at runtime using fs.watchFile
file_indicators: Obfuscated JavaScript in main package file
References to file-sharing endpoints such as telegra.ph, uguu.se, catbox.moe, pomf2.lain.la, uploadcare.com, tmpfiles.org, itzpire.site, skizo.tech
fs.watchFile usage targeting __filename in JavaScript files
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor JavaScript packages for creation of form-data from arbitrary file buffers and automated HTTP POST requests to known file-sharing endpoints, especially if these actions occur without user interaction. Flag any use of fs.watchFile on the package's own file (__filename), and inspect for obfuscated code or hardcoded references to suspicious upload URLs. Network monitoring should alert on outbound POST requests to the listed file-sharing domains. Correlate these behaviors to identify covert data exfiltration attempts.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code captures screenshots and webcam images using system APIs or npm modules, then exfiltrates the captured media to a remote server via network requests, resulting in unauthorized surveillance.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing the screen and camera without user consent and sending the data externally is a hallmark of spyware and privacy violation.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages should not access or exfiltrate screen or camera data unless explicitly designed for such purposes with user awareness and consent.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Video conferencing or screenshot tools may access these resources, but only with user consent and without silent exfiltration to unknown servers.
key_indicators: Use of screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules for image capture
Silent capture of screenshots or webcam images without user notification
Network exfiltration of image data to remote servers
Absence of user prompts or consent dialogs for camera/screen access

execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript file or auxiliary modules

package_info.why_malicious: The package is considered malicious because it abuses a legitimate password-recovery tool (ChromePass) to steal credentials from Google Chrome, and provides additional capabilities such as unauthorized screen and camera access, directory enumeration, and remote shell command execution. These behaviors are not expected in legitimate npm packages and indicate clear intent to exfiltrate sensitive user data and enable remote control of the victim's system.

attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of malicious code at runtime

attack_chain.action: At runtime, the package executes ChromePass.exe to extract Chrome passwords and exfiltrates them to a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential theft and exfiltration

attack_chain.action: The package captures screenshots and webcam images, then exfiltrates them to a remote server.
attack_chain.leads_to: Surveillance and privacy violation

attack_chain.leads_to: Reconnaissance for further exploitation

attack_chain.action: The package enables remote shell command execution, allowing attackers to control the victim's system and maintain persistence.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of ChromePass.exe or similar credential extraction tools from within npm packages
Silent screenshot or webcam capture using screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules followed by network exfiltration
Automated directory listing of user or system directories and exfiltration of file lists
Remote command execution via child_process.exec or similar APIs, especially when commands originate from network sources
file_indicators: Bundled or downloaded ChromePass.exe binary within the package directory
Creation of temporary files such as passwords.txt in user-accessible directories
Unusual or unauthorized use of screenshot-desktop or node-webcam modules in non-UI npm packages
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known command-and-control or exfiltration domains immediately after package installation or execution
HTTP POST requests containing credential dumps, screenshots, webcam images, or directory listings

detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that execute external binaries such as ChromePass.exe, access camera or screen APIs, or perform directory listing and exfiltration. Flag packages that initiate outbound network connections immediately after installation or at runtime, especially those sending sensitive files, images, or command outputs. Use endpoint security tools to detect suspicious process execution and network activity originating from node.js processes, and correlate with the presence of bundled binaries or unauthorized use of system resources.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, play-share.js sets up an HTTP server on port 3004 that executes arbitrary system commands received via the 'cmd' query parameter, returning the output to the remote attacker and enabling persistent remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Establishing a local HTTP server for arbitrary command execution is a classic RAT/backdoor pattern, providing attackers with persistent, unauthorized access to the victim system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate package should expose a remote code execution interface or listen for attacker-supplied commands on a local port.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate HTTP servers do not execute arbitrary system commands based on unauthenticated query parameters.
key_indicators: Command execution via unauthenticated query parameter
Returns command output to remote requester

package_info.why_malicious: The package contains heavily obfuscated JavaScript code that functions as a dropper and remote access trojan (RAT). It performs environment checks to selectively infect targets, downloads and executes additional payloads, and establishes a persistent HTTP server for arbitrary remote code execution, all without user consent. The malicious logic is triggered during test or runtime, bypassing normal package behavior and enabling persistent attacker control.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed and test script is triggered, executing the obfuscated loader in index.js.
attack_chain.leads_to: Loader (bind) function is executed, initiating the attack chain.

attack_chain.action: Loader (bind) function asynchronously launches dropper (start) and persistence (share) routines.
attack_chain.leads_to: Dropper logic (start) and persistence (share) are triggered.

attack_chain.action: Dropper logic (start) performs environment checks, then downloads and/or executes arbitrary payloads or commands.
attack_chain.leads_to: Payload is executed or remote binary is downloaded and run, enabling code execution.

attack_chain.action: Persistence routine (share) launches play-share.js as a detached background process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Background RAT server is established and runs independently.

attack_chain.action: RAT server (play-share.js) listens on port 3004, executing attacker-supplied commands via HTTP requests.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains persistent remote code execution on the victim machine.

behavioral_signatures: Execution of obfuscated JavaScript code as part of npm test or runtime scripts
Immediate invocation of local obfuscated modules with side effects
Detached background process launching local scripts (e.g., play-share.js)
Creation of HTTP server on non-standard port (e.g., 3004) for command execution
Dynamic download and execution of remote payloads or binaries
Creation and use of lock files (e.g., node.compress.lock.log) to control execution flow
file_indicators: lib/play-share.js (obfuscated, sets up HTTP server for RCE)
network_indicators: HTTP server listening on port 3004 for incoming requests
Outbound HTTP GET requests to attacker-controlled URLs for payload download
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for obfuscated JavaScript files executed via npm lifecycle or test scripts. Flag packages that immediately invoke local obfuscated modules or launch detached background processes. Detect creation of local HTTP servers on non-standard ports (e.g., 3004) and monitor for command execution via HTTP query parameters. Identify dynamic download and execution of binaries, especially when triggered by hidden or obfuscated logic. Look for the presence of suspicious lock files or temporary executables (e.g., node.compress.exe, node.compress.lock.log). Network monitoring should alert on unexpected local HTTP servers and outbound requests to untrusted or attacker-controlled domains.
